abstract: This lecture on antepartum fetal surveillance covers its purpose to prevent stillbirth by detecting fetal hypoxia, the main modalities (nonstress test, biophysical profile, modified BPP, contraction stress test, umbilical artery Doppler), and the indications and timing for high-risk pregnancies. The speaker reviews criteria for test interpretation, such as NST reactivity requiring 15 bpm accelerations for 15 seconds within 20 minutes, and BPP scoring with each component graded 2 or 0. Common indications discussed include chronic hypertension on medication, pregestational or medication-controlled gestational diabetes, fetal growth restriction, and advanced maternal age, with most surveillance starting at 32 weeks. Case examples reinforce when to initiate testing and highlight pitfalls such as not testing stable maternal conditions.
key_points: Antepartum fetal surveillance aims to identify fetuses at risk for stillbirth by detecting hypoxia/acidosis.
The nonstress test (NST) requires accelerations of 15 bpm for 15 seconds within 20 minutes for reactivity; for fetuses <32 weeks, a lower threshold applies.
Biophysical profile (BPP) scores five components (fetal breathing, movement, tone, amniotic fluid, NST) each 2 if normal, 0 if abnormal; total 8-10 is reassuring, 6 is equivocal, <6 is abnormal.
Modified BPP combines a reactive NST with a normal amniotic fluid index (≥5 cm) and is less resource-intensive.
Umbilical artery Doppler is essential for fetal growth restriction; absent or reverse end-diastolic flow indicates severe hypoxia and requires urgent management.
Indications for surveillance include chronic hypertension on medication, pregestational or medication-controlled gestational diabetes (GDM A2), and fetal growth restriction.
Surveillance generally starts at 32 weeks for most high-risk conditions, but earlier for severe disease or abnormal Doppler findings.
For diet-controlled gestational diabetes (GDM A1), advanced maternal age (≥40), and stable cardiac/pulmonary/seizure disorders, routine surveillance is not clearly recommended.
Decreased fetal movement warrants a single workup with NST/BPP; if reassuring, serial testing is not needed.
Postterm pregnancy (≥41 weeks) should prompt consideration of surveillance and induction.
Antepartum fetal surveillance should start at 32 weeks for most high-risk conditions.
Conditions requiring surveillance include hypertension, gestational diabetes, and fetal growth restriction.
